Confound

kuhn-FOWND · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To confound to cause confusion or bewilderment in someone.

The riddle at the escape room's final door confounded every team that attempted it that weekend.

Worked Example

The auditors were confounded by the company's books, which somehow balanced perfectly despite three years of missing receipts.

Confound describes a deep, often frustrating confusion -- something that genuinely stumps a person, not just a passing question.

How Confound Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

baffle

baffle: to completely confuse or puzzle

perplex

perplex: to confuse or puzzle someone

Antonyms

clarify

clarify: to make something clear and easier to understand

enlighten

enlighten: to give someone greater understanding

How Strong Is It? — puzzle → confound → stupefy

puzzle vs. confound

puzzle vs. confound: Puzzle describes a milder curiosity or confusion, without the deep frustration that confound often implies.

stupefy vs. confound

stupefy vs. confound: Stupefy goes further than confound, describing a confusion so total it leaves someone stunned and unable to think at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — con-

prefix — con-: with, together (intensifying) (Latin)

root — fund-

root — fund-: to pour, to mix together (Latin fundere)

Put it together

Put it together: Confound comes from Latin confundere ('to pour together, to mix up') -- the exact same Latin ancestor as the everyday word confuse, just borrowed into English twice, through two different paths.

Use the root in a new word: confuse

Use the root in a new word: confuse: Two nearly identical road signs confuse drivers at the exit every single day.

Root Check

Word Choice

Confound and confuse share the exact same Latin ancestor, confundere -- English just borrowed the word twice, once through French (confound) and once directly from Latin (confuse). They're practically cousins.
